title: U.K. government ordered to reveal secret Apple backdoor demand
content:
Macworld





The U.K.’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal today ruled that the British government must confirm that it demanded access to Apple customers’ data in 2025.
Early last year, the Washington Post was tipped off about the secret order, or “technical capability notice,” which ordered Apple to “create a back door allowing [U.K. authorities] to retrieve all the content any Apple user worldwide has uploaded to the cloud.” At the time, we warned that such an order would instantly compromise the security of more than two billion Apple users across the globe.
Apple resisted, choosing to remove the ADP feature from U.K. iPhones rather than comply with the order, and it was subsequently reported that British politicians had given up on the scheme. But while it was common knowledge that the attempt had been made, the Home Office refused to acknowledge this, arguing that revealing the existence of the order would damage national security and the public interest.
Apple itself was not permitted to disclose that it had received a technical capability notice. Until now the company has adhered to this even while commenting in carefully non-specific terms on the situation. At one point, for example, it stated that “we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products, and we never will” without actually confirming it had been ordered to do so in this case.
But now, finally, as TechCrunch reports, the national security argument has been put to rest.
Having noted that “anyone with even a passing interest in this topic already knows that the respondent has served a technical capability notice on Apple,” the three judges indicate that they “reject the respondent’s contention that it would be damaging to national security to confirm the fact that the respondent has given Apple a technical capability notice.”
It should be noted that this judgment refers to the existence of the order rather than its specific details. The judges say this is “another matter” which “is better addressed separately.” The case, in other words, is not finished yet.

title: Apple job listing gives away proactive agentic AI project
content:
Macworld





A new job listing for a Senior Engineering Manager at Apple’s Cupertino campus has given away an open secret: Apple is working on an autonomous, proactive AI agent.
“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the listing begins. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”
AI agents that operate continuously and proactively in the background are the latest hot item, and some think are the next big frontier in consumer AI. It’s the natural successor to chatbots, and is often perceived as the big step that will get the whole world hooked on AI.

Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.
 Apple job listing




Currently, AI agents are extremely popular in the App Store. Meta’s Muse is the #2 free app, behind only TikTok. Chatbots that have added agentic capabilities hold other top spots: ChatGPT is #3, Claude is #5, and Gemini is #7.
Each of these has varying degrees of autonomy, and many of the Mac apps from these companies can access your Mac’s data and operate its app. Google’s Gemini Mac app was just updated to be able to use your Mac for you, for example.
Apple’s job posting makes it clear that the company is building its own similar product. The job description is as follows:
People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service. We’re building AI agents that can do the same. We’re a team of engineers, AI applied researchers, and systems specialists working on general-purpose computer-use agents. These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way. 
As a senior leader in this org, you will own the technical direction and delivery of our agent platform and the AI capabilities built on it. You will lead and develop a team of managers and engineers. You will also build the AI and systems talent that will define what we can ship next. You’ll work closely with partner teams across Siri, UI frameworks, and AFM and more. Your job is to turn their capabilities, and ours, into agents that are capable, reliable, and safe.
The posted job listing is for a senior management position, someone who will, “Set the technical vision, roadmap, and quality bar for AI agents that work across apps, browsers, terminals, code, and APIs.” If that is the case, and Apple is trying to assemble its team and direct the vision for the project now, then it is at least a year behind its competitors. Competing services have proactive and autonomous AI agents available to consumers today–even if Apple races ahead at top speed, it’s hard to imagine a similar product reaching users until at least the fall of 2027, by which time Meta, OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic will be on their second or third generation of consumer AI agents.

title: Gemini can now tap into your Mac for app automation
content:
Macworld





Google announced on Thursday that its Gemini Mac app will soon get Computer Use and be able to automate Mac tasks with your installed apps without direct input. It can do all of this in the background while you do other work.
Gemini users will be able to enter a description of what needs to be done, and Gemini will do all the work in an isolated background window with a live preview in the app. You’ll be able to do other things on the Mac while Gemini is at work. Examples of the types of tasks that can be done, cited by Google, include batch color-grading photos, setting up complex 3D scenes, automated PDF form entries, data scraped from screenshots and then placed in a presentation, and batch analysis of items in a photo.
Google states that users will be able to control what apps Gemini can access, as well as pause or stop actions, and approve key actions before they are executed. While users have been able to use Apple’s Shortcuts or AppleScript to automate actions, this provides a straightforward, plain-language way for people who are intimidated by those tools.
The new automation support is being rolled out gradually as per Google’s usual updates. When I installed Gemini before writing this story, I downloaded the older version that does not have this new feature, so it kept failing when I tried to use Gemini to automate tasks in Pixelmator Pro, QuickTime Player, and the Finder. At one point, Gemini said that the version I have (version 1.147.5.1526) has “a built-in security boundary in Gemini’s Mac sandbox,” which is presumably being modified for the automation support in the new version. If you try to download the new version and keep getting the old one (like me), check back at a later time.

title: I already hit Apple’s ‘generous’ daily Siri AI usage limit
content:
Macworld





You’re probably vaguely familiar with AI chatbots’ usage limits or tokens, which are dictated by your plan and the type of requests you make. When you hit a limit, you typically need to wait for a few hours or days until full functionality is restored. 
In the meantime, your queries are handled by a less capable model that may not be as fast or accurate. While Siri AI on iOS 27 operates similarly, we haven’t had to deal with usage limits until iOS 27.3, when Apple rolled out daily usage limits based on iCloud storage tiers. However, unlike other services, Apple hasn’t been very clear about how tokens are tallied. So imagine my surprise when I hit one with a relatively simple workflow, despite subscribing to the 2TB iCloud+ plan, which multiplies the quota by 5X. It’s still unclear what the limits are, but they appear to be significantly more stringent than those of other platforms I’ve used.
It all started when I was working on an upcoming Macworld article revolving around Siri AI on Apple TV. Over the course of 20 minutes, I made numerous straightforward Siri requests on tvOS once every minute or so. Most of them were as simple as “send my friend a text,” while the more complex tasks included surfacing iPhone file names and reminders on the big screen and installing an app. Neither I nor the other family members on my account had generated any media in Image Playground (does anyone?), nor had we used Siri to solve any deeply analytical problems or used any third-party apps or shortcuts that rely on Apple’s AI models.
Interestingly, Apple claims that Siri AI includes a “generous daily usage limit” for all users, whether or not they subscribe to iCloud+. So one would assume that the 5x increase included with my $9.99/month 2TB iCloud+ plan would be sufficient for direct questions, basic commands, minimal proofreading, and the like. Apparently not. The Siri app now displays a “daily limit reached” banner on my iPhone, barring me from making any advanced requests until tomorrow.
For reference, advanced requests include plain multi-step queries such as “check the weather and text it to my mom.” Instead, I now have to ask about the forecast and have it send the message separately—as the downgraded Siri experience cannot handle the complexity of both at once for the rest of the day—or upgrade to the $29.99/month 6TB iCloud+ plan. 
Meanwhile, my iPad and Mac now also warn that I’m approaching their respective daily request limits, as my iPhone and Apple TV have seemingly exhausted the shared pool. That’s by far the most restrictive limit I’ve ever encountered with any other popular AI chatbot. So unless you’re spending a fortune on iCloud each month, be careful with how much you talk to Siri—it could cost you.

title: iPhone Duo vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8: Which is Better?
content:
A couple of months before the iPhone Duo came out, Samsung launched the Galaxy Z Fold8. It's Samsung's widest and shortest foldable to date, with Samsung adopting an aspect ratio closer to the ‌iPhone Duo‌'s than its previous foldable smartphones. Since the Z Fold8 was clearly designed to compete with the ‌iPhone Duo‌, we thought we'd compare the two devices.

Subscribe to the MacRumors YouTube channel for more videos.

The Galaxy Z Fold8 and ‌iPhone Duo‌ are similar in size, but the Fold8 is noticeably lighter. It's about 50 grams lighter than the ‌iPhone Duo‌, and it makes a difference when you're holding it. It's lighter because it's thinner than the ‌iPhone Duo‌ when folded and unfolded. The Z Fold8 is 6mm taller and around 3mm narrower, though both have a 7.6-inch inner display.

The ‌iPhone Duo‌ has a heftier feel and a more premium build, plus it has rounded corners that feel nicer in the hand than the Z Fold8's sharper, rectangular corners.

Apple used a matte nano-texture display for the ‌iPhone Duo‌, and that's likely something we're going to see Android smartphone makers imitate in their future foldables. The matte display goes a long way toward minimizing the visibility of the crease. Apple also put the camera on the inner display under the screen, which is something Samsung experimented with in earlier models and then abandoned.

Under-display front cameras are generally lower resolution than standard cameras, and there have been complaints about the quality of the ‌iPhone Duo‌'s inner front camera. The Z Fold8 has a more traditional hole-punch camera that's better quality.

similar face unlock option, and it's coming in iOS 27.3. Face unlock is less secure than the Face ID system used for Apple's other iPhones, but it is more convenient than Touch ID for some users.

Neither smartphone has a telephoto camera, so both Apple and Samsung compromised on camera quality. The ‌iPhone Duo‌ has a 48-megapixel Main camera and a 48-megapixel Ultra Wide, while the Z Fold8 has 50-megapixel wide and ultra wide cameras. The main difference in image quality is the computational processing each smartphone offers, so which one is "better" comes down to your preference for white balance, saturation, tone, and similar factors.

Apple Pencil, but the Z Fold8 doesn't work with Samsung's S Pen options.

Since Samsung has been making foldable smartphones for years, developers have had more time to update their apps for the form factor. Most Android apps already work well, while we're still waiting for many developers to update their apps for the Duo. Samsung is also ahead on multitasking, with the option to use three apps at once and support for pop-up windows and a taskbar.

Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold8 is slightly cheaper than the ‌iPhone Duo‌, with pricing starting at $1,899.99 while the Duo starts at $1,999, but deciding between them will come down to your operating system preference and device ecosystem. If you're accustomed to iOS and have an Apple Watch, Mac, and other Apple devices, there's little reason to choose a Samsung smartphone. The same goes for Samsung users who have other Galaxy devices.

title: The iMac might be stuck with an LCD forever
content:
Macworld





Apple’s devices are slowly switching over to OLED displays. It started with the Apple Watch, then the iPhone X and the iPad Pro, and most recently OLED finally made it to the Mac with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. It’s been a long process that started with smaller devices and has gradually made its way into larger ones, but according to The Elec, it’s going to be a while before we see OLED in Apple’s biggest screens.
According to the report, Apple is considering either delaying or canceling its plans for an OLED iMac. The reason: OLED panels that meet Apple’s standards are too expensive right now. Since Apple’s all-in-one “sells in smaller volumes than smartphones or laptops,” it’s been more difficult to “maintain competitive pricing if expensive OLED panels are adopted,” according to The Elec.
Another reason that may have influenced Apple’s decision is the sales of the iPad Pro, which was upgraded in 2024 with a tandem OLED display. OLED’s higher cost cause the iPad Pro’s price to increase, which The Elec says resulted in “sales below expectations.” And more more reason for the change of plans is that Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is “reassessing the commercial viability” of OLED.
When Apple introduced the OLED iPad in 2024, the price increased $200. The 11-inch iPad Pro before OLED was $799, then in 2024 it increased to $999, while the 13-inch iPad Pro jumped from $1,099 to $1,299. Similarly Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is $400 more than the MacBook Pro with a mini-LED display. Compounding things is the RAM and storage shortages, which have pushed iPad and Mac prices even higher. Apple just released the M6 iMac without increasing the price further.
iMac development hasn’t shut down completely. The Elec states that Apple has plans for a new LCD-based model based on the current display technology for “around 2029,” which would likely be an M8 chip. Perhaps by then, the cost for OLED will have come down, and Apple can revisit its iMac OLED plans for 2030, but you probably shouldn’t get your hopes up.

title: UK can't hide that it tried ordering Apple to allow access to user data
content:
A tribunal has ruled in favor of Apple and against UK government's attempt to keep secret it ordering backdoor access to encrypted iPhone data.


UK Parliament - image credit: Parliament
Apple is the firm that refused to create a way for the FBI to gain access to users' encrypted iPhone data, so it was never likely to do it for a foreign country. Nonetheless, the UK first tried back in 2016, and then in 2024 changed its own laws to allow it to make such demands secretly.
The UK then ordered Apple to create such a backdoor and used that law to forbid the company from revealing the order. The government issued what it calls a Technical Capability Notice (TCN), which, if Apple had complied, would give it access to any or all users' encrypted data worldwide.

PRICES CHECKED NOVEMBER 19 2026 – Deals change quickly, so we will update this page throughout November
Black Friday is a great time to buy AirPods, with retailers competing to offer discounts across Apple’s earbuds and over-ear headphones. Previous sales have brought substantial savings on established models, clearance bargains on older generations, and even discounts on newly released AirPods. But the biggest percentage saving doesn’t necessarily mean the best buy: an older pair needs to be sufficiently cheaper than its replacement to justify missing out on newer features.
Last Black Friday, standard AirPods 4 briefly dropped to $69 in the U.S., while the noise-canceling version fell to $99 – an $80 saving. Even the then-new AirPods Pro 3 received a discount of around $30, while older AirPods Pro 2 reached approximately $139 before selling out. AirPods Max were available for around $400, roughly $150 below their regular price. U.K. savings were more modest, with AirPods 4 at £99 and AirPods Pro 2 at £169, although stock frequently ran out.
This year, we’d watch AirPods Pro 3 and AirPods Max 2 for meaningful discounts, while remaining AirPods 4 and AirPods Pro 2 stock could bring some of the biggest clearance savings. The recently released AirPods 5 may see smaller reductions, making it especially important to compare their price with discounted Pro models. Below, we explain which AirPods to choose and how the offers compare with previous discounts. For savings on Macs, iPads, Apple Watch and more, see our best Apple Black Friday deals.
Apple’s owb Black Friday offer runs November 27–30, 2026. Buy eligible AirPods directly from Apple and you’ll receive a gift card to use on a future purchase. More details here: Apple Black Friday 2026: Up to $300/£240 in gift cards – full list of eligible products.




Which AirPods should you buy this Black Friday?


AirPods Pro 3 – Our best overall choice

				
					

				
			
Apple




AirPods Pro 3 are especially worth considering if you want strong noise cancellation, a secure in-ear fit, or Apple’s hearing-health features. Their foam-infused ear tips help improve the fit, while an in-ear heart-rate sensor adds another reason to choose them over standard AirPods. Battery life is rated at up to eight hours with noise cancellation enabled.
For most buyers looking for noise-isolating earbuds, these would be our first choice. Older AirPods Pro 2 are worth considering only when the clearance savings are substantial.
U.S. Black Friday price:  Amazon has already slashed almost $70 off the AirPods Pro 3, but we expect the price to go lower. We hope they’ll return to their all-time low of $169 by Black Friday. 
U.K. Black Friday price: Earlier in November, AirPods Pro 3 were £30 off in the U.K., before rising to £200, then dropping down to £174, only to return to £200. This is one to watch because that price is going up and down like a Swanee whistle. Apple’s £40 gift card offers better value currently. 
Apple’s deal: You can get a $50/£40 gift card with your purchase. 






AirPods 5 – Best for buyers who prefer earbuds without silicone tips

				
					

				
			
Apple




AirPods 5 offer a lower-cost entry point and an open-ear design for people who don’t like silicone-tipped earbuds. They include Active Noise Cancellation as standard, alongside Transparency mode and Adaptive Audio.
Check which charging case you’re buying. The Wireless Charging Case package adds wireless charging, longer battery life, a Find My speaker, and volume adjustment by swiping the stems. It’s our preferred package when the price difference is small.
U.S. Black Friday price: We’ve not seen a discount yet on the AirPods 5.
U.K. Black Friday price:  You can get £20 off the AirPods 5 in the U.K. This is the same ‘saving’ as Apple’s gift card, but you get the £20 saving upfront. 
Apple’s deal: Get $25/£20 gift card with the purchase of AirPods 5. 






AirPods Max 2 – Best for over-ear listening

				
					

				
			
Apple




AirPods Max 2 are the option to consider if you specifically want over-ear headphones. The March 2026 update introduced Apple’s H2 chip and improved noise cancellation, while retaining the premium design and a choice of colors.
We find them difficult to recommend at full price, so the size of the discount matters. Compare any offer with previous sale prices rather than judging it solely against Apple’s asking price.
U.S. Black Friday price:  Amazon has the AirPods Max 2 for $449, that’s $99 off. They could still go lower though. 
U.K. Black Friday price:  The AirPods Max 2 are £449 at Amazon – that’s £50 off. You can get the same deal at AO and Boots. Apple’s £60 gift card offers better value, currently. 
Apple’s deal: Get $75/£60 gift card with the purchase of AirPods Max 2. 






Other AirPods – Buy only at a worthwhile clearance price

				
					

				
			
Apple




AirPods 4 and AirPods Pro 2 can still be worth considering, but compare them with the discounted prices of their replacements. A large reduction from an older model’s launch price can disguise a small saving over a newer, more capable pair.
Check the exact generation, charging case, condition, and seller before buying. For more help choosing, read our AirPods buying guide.
U.S. Black Friday price:  There’s $150 off the former price of the AirPods Pro 2 at Walmart, meaning you can grab a pair for just $149.
U.K. Black Friday price:  You can get the AirPods 4 with ANC for £109 at John Lewis – but that’s only £10 less than AirPods 5, so we’d recommend waiting for that price to go even lower.






Other headphones – Worthy AirPods alternatives

				
					

				
			
Beats




If AirPods aren’t in your budget, Apple also sells a line of Beats headphones and earbuds that offer many of the same features for a lower price, including the popular on-ear Solo 4 and Powerbeats Pro 2. With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need AirPods immediately. But the sales now stretch across much of November, so you don’t necessarily need to wait for Black Friday itself. If an early offer is close to a model’s previous low, it can be worth taking: last year’s best deals frequently sold out, and popular offers could go quickly again.
Previous sale prices provide useful benchmarks. We’ve seen AirPods Pro 3 reach $169, while AirPods Max 2 fell to $399 during June Prime Day. An offer above those prices may still be worth considering, but a reduction from Apple’s regular price doesn’t automatically make it an exceptional deal.
For AirPods 5, waiting for a discount makes sense if you aren’t in a hurry: they didn’t receive a significant reduction during October Prime Day. With AirPods Max 2, we’d hold out for a substantial saving rather than pay full price.
Compare retailers, too. Amazon isn’t always cheapest: Walmart and Best Buy also compete on AirPods pricing, while Argos offered competitive U.K. deals last year. Our guide to the best time to buy AirPods has more advice on purchase timing.






Should you buy an old pair of AirPods? 
Older-generation AirPods can be a good buy at the right clearance price. Compare their actual selling price with the discounted price of their replacement, rather than focusing on the percentage saving from an old launch price. A substantial discount can make an older pair worthwhile; a small difference may leave you sacrificing useful features for little saving.
AirPods 4 are harder to recommend now that AirPods 5 include Active Noise Cancellation as standard, starting at the same $129 price previously charged for AirPods 4 without ANC. Check which AirPods 4 version you’re buying—there were models with and without noise cancellation—and look for a substantial saving over AirPods 5.
AirPods Pro 2 remain worth considering if they’re significantly cheaper than Pro 3. However, the newer model improves fit, noise cancellation, and battery life, while adding heart-rate sensing. Compare their sale prices carefully: a strong Pro 3 discount could make the older pair’s clearance offer less attractive.
The original AirPods Max also need a substantial discount to justify choosing them over Max 2. The newer headphones add the H2 chip, improved noise cancellation, and features including Adaptive Audio and Conversation Awareness. Check the generation rather than relying on the charging port alone: the original AirPods Max were also sold in a USB-C version.
Buying older stock new is different from buying used or refurbished AirPods. For those pairs, check the stated condition, charging case, warranty, and returns policy, and buy from a reputable seller. Be cautious about battery condition and unusually low marketplace prices, since convincing counterfeits can resemble genuine AirPods. Our guide explains how to spot fake AirPods.
For more advice, see our AirPods buying guide and guide to the best time to buy AirPods.






AirPods deals to avoid

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Check exactly what an offer includes before comparing prices. Different charging-case packages can affect features and value, so make sure you’re comparing equivalent versions. Also check any spending requirements, contracts, or rebates attached to offers advertising “free” AirPods.
Judge the price against previous selling prices as well as the advertised discount. A large saving from the recommended retail price doesn’t necessarily mean a particularly good deal if retailers regularly charge less.
Check whether the listing is for a new, refurbished, or used pair. For used or refurbished AirPods, look for clear information about condition, warranty, and returns coverage. Battery condition deserves particular caution: a low purchase price may be less attractive if listening time has deteriorated.
Finally, check who is selling and dispatching your order, particularly when shopping through a marketplace. Unusually low prices from unfamiliar sellers warrant caution, since counterfeit AirPods can look convincing. Our guide explains how to tell if AirPods are fake.






How we choose AirPods deals
Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on AirPods reviews. We consider sound quality, noise cancellation, comfort, battery life, and everyday use – not just the specifications or advertised saving.
Our testing helps us explain which features are worth paying for. For example, our AirPods Pro 3 review assessed how securely the redesigned ear tips stayed in place during exercise, checked battery life against Apple’s claims, and evaluated the heart-rate sensor. Our AirPods Max 2 review weighed their excellent sound and noise cancellation against drawbacks including weight and the Smart Case.
We combine those findings with current prices and previous lows to judge whether an offer represents good value. Our Best AirPods guide explains why the most expensive model isn’t necessarily the best choice for everyone: fit, listening habits, and the features you need all matter.

title: Tomorrow Marks the End of a 28-Year Era at Apple
content:
Apple previously announced that the Apple Support Community discussion forums for user-to-user tech support will be permanently closing this Friday, November 20. The forums have existed in some form for 28 years. It is the end of an era.


It is our understanding that the forums will eventually be removed entirely, meaning that existing posts will no longer be visible. However, it is not clear if that will happen immediately on November 20 or at a later date.

final message posted to the site appears to have been submitted on November 10 at 5:49 p.m. Pacific Time. On the English forums, this change happened abruptly, leaving members with no chance to post farewell messages.

The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.

Apple Support site. 

The forums have a 28-year history. Apple offered an online discussion forum for user-to-user tech support since 1998, when it launched the Apple Tech Exchange. The forums were renamed to Apple Discussions in 2000, and then to the Apple Support Communities in 2011, before taking on their current Apple Support Community name in 2022.


Apple informed MacRumors that it decided to sunset the Apple Support Community after a careful evaluation of strategy and customer needs. 

MacRumors Forums and Reddit, and customers can continue to contact Apple Support.

PRICES CHECKED 19 NOVEMBER, 2026 – Deals change quickly, so we will update this page throughout November.
Black Friday is a great time to buy an Apple Watch, with retailers discounting everything from the affordable SE to the premium Ultra. Last year’s U.S. offers included $50 off the SE 3, up to $70 off the then-new Series 11, and $100 off the Ultra 3. Older models brought bigger savings, including $150 off the Series 10 and $200 off the Ultra 2. In the U.K., clearance offers were particularly attractive: the Series 10 was up to £130 off at Currys, while Argos cut £200 from the Ultra 2’s original price.
October Prime Day brought discounts on this year’s models, too. In the U.S., the 42mm Series 12 fell to $349, the 40mm SE 3 to $199, and the Ultra 4 to $774 – savings of $50, $50, and $25 respectively. U.K. highlights included the SE 3 at £199 and the previous-generation Series 11 at £259.
This Black Friday, we’d look for discounts on the Series 12, our pick as the best Apple Watch for most people, the SE 3 for an affordable entry point, and the Ultra 4 for longer battery life and outdoor features. Remaining Series 11 and Ultra 3 stock could offer particularly good value if priced sufficiently below their replacements. Below, we explain which offers are worth taking and when to wait; for savings across Apple’s other products, see our best Apple Black Friday deals.
From November 27 through November 30, Apple will include a $50 U.S. or £40 U.K. Apple Gift Card with an eligible Apple Watch Series 12 or SE 3 bought directly from Apple. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes with a $100 U.S. or £80 U.K. gift card. See our guide to Apple’s Black Friday shopping event for the full offer.
Which Apple Watch should you buy this Black Friday?


Apple Watch Series 12 – Our best overall choice

				
					

				
			

Apple




The Series 12 is the Apple Watch we recommend for most people. It combines Apple’s new Health Sensing System, more frequent heart-rate measurements, a Readiness score, and a tougher display with up to 24 hours of battery life.
A worthwhile Black Friday discount could make it an attractive purchase, but compare it with remaining Series 11 stock. The older model has the same quoted battery life, so a substantial saving may outweigh the newer health features.
U.S. Black Friday price: Amazon has already discounted the 42mm GPS Series 12 to $329, saving  $70 and the best price we’ve ever seen. The 46mm version is also $70 off.
U.K. Black Friday price: We didn’t see Series 12 discounts during October Prime Day, and so far this November there have been no price drops, but we are hopeful. We have only seen discounts on older models so far.
Apple’s deal: Apple will give $50 U.S. or £40 U.K. Apple Gift Card with an eligible Apple Watch Series 12. Amazon’s $70 Series 12 discount in the U.S. is worth more than Apple’s $50 gift card.






Apple Watch Ultra 4 – Best for battery life and outdoor adventures

				
					

				
			

Apple




The Ultra 4 is our choice for endurance athletes, outdoor enthusiasts, and buyers who prioritize battery life. It offers up to 50 hours of normal use, satellite communication, precision dual-frequency GPS, diving features, and Apple’s new Health Sensing System.
It’s more watch than most people need. Compare it with the Ultra 3, though, which retains many of its outdoor features but has a shorter 42-hour battery-life rating.
U.S. Black Friday price: October Prime Day brought the Ultra 4 down to $774, a $25 saving. This November we’ve already seen the Apple Watch Ultra 4 for $699.99 on Amazon: that’s almost $100 off. However, the price is now up to $774 at Amazon, so we recommend watching for the price to dip again.
U.K. Black Friday price: The Ultra 4 remained at its full £749 price during October Prime Day, but we’ve already seen it drop by £30 to £719 at Amazon.
Apple’s deal: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes with a $100 U.S. or £80 U.K. Apple gift card if you buy direct from Apple.






Apple Watch SE 3 – Our best budget choice

				
					

				
			
Apple / Amazon




The SE 3 is the best-value option for buyers who want the core Apple Watch experience. It includes an always-on display, temperature sensing, fast charging, and the S10 chip, but lacks ECG, blood oxygen monitoring, and the newer Health Sensing System.
It remains part of Apple’s current lineup despite launching in 2025. A strong Black Friday offer could make it an excellent affordable purchase, although its previous discounts mean there’s little reason to settle for a token reduction.
U.S. Black Friday price: Both last Black Friday and October Prime Day brought the 40mm GPS model to $199 and the 44mm version to $229 – $50 below their regular prices. Already, the U.S. price is $199, $50 off at Amazon.
U.K. Black Friday price: Black Friday 2025 and October Prime Day brought the 40mm GPS model to £199 and the 44mm version to £229, saving £20. So far we haven’t seen any price drops for Black Friday 2026.
Apple’s deal: Apple will give $50 U.S. or £40 U.K. Apple Gift Card with an eligible Apple Watch SE 3 bought directly from Apple. 






Apple Watch Ultra 3 – Best clearance option for outdoor enthusiasts

				
					

				
			
Apple




The Ultra 3 is worth considering if you want a rugged Apple Watch without paying for the latest model. It offers satellite communication, dual-frequency GPS, diving features, and up to 42 hours of battery life.
You give up the Ultra 4’s longer battery life and newer Health Sensing System. Compare their actual selling prices: the Ultra 3 needs to be sufficiently cheaper to justify choosing the older generation.
U.S. Black Friday price: Last Black Friday, the Ultra 3 fell to $699, $100 saving. Our October Prime Day coverage found only used models, so it didn’t identify a comparable new-stock offer. So far this November we’ve seen the Apple Watch Ultra 3 for $649, but that’s now out of stock.

Apple Watch Series 11 – Best clearance option for everyday use

				
					

				
			
Apple Watch Series 11




The Series 11 could be a better-value everyday watch than the Series 12 if the price gap is large enough. It has the same quoted 24-hour battery life, although it lacks the newer Health Sensing System and Audio Intelligence features.
For buyers who don’t need those additions, a substantial clearance discount could be more useful than a small saving on the latest model.

Should you buy an Apple Watch now or wait for a better deal?
With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need an Apple Watch immediately. But sales stretch across much of November, so you don’t necessarily need to wait for Black Friday itself. If an early offer matches or comes close to a previous low for the same model and configuration, it can be worth taking – particularly if you want a specific size, color, or band combination.
October Prime Day prices provide useful benchmarks. In the U.S., the Series 12 fell to $349 for the 42mm GPS model and $399 for the 46mm version, while the Ultra 4 reached $774. The SE 3 was $199 in 40mm and $229 in 44mm. Those SE prices also appeared last Black Friday, so we’d look for offers matching or beating them. In the U.K., October highlights included the 40mm SE 3 at £199 and the older 42mm Series 11 at £259.
The Series 12 and Ultra 4 only arrived in September, so finding a better price is the main reason to wait. If you don’t need a watch immediately, those previous offers give you a useful starting point for deciding whether to buy now or hold out.
Compare retailers, too. Last Black Friday, Walmart offered $150 off the Series 10, while U.K. shoppers could find up to £130 off at Currys and £200 off the Ultra 2’s original price at Argos. Our guide to the best time to buy an Apple Watch has more advice on choosing when to purchase.






Should you buy an older Apple Watch?

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Don’t assume an older Apple Watch is a bad buy. The Series 11 and Ultra 3 are only one generation old and can make excellent purchases if they’re substantially cheaper than the Series 12 or Ultra 4. Both retain many of their replacements’ core features, although you miss the newer Health Sensing System and, with the Ultra 3, the Ultra 4’s longer battery life.
Compare actual selling prices, matching case size, material, connectivity, and band where possible. A $50 difference between a Series 11 and Series 12 may not be enough to justify giving up the newer model’s health features, whereas a substantially larger saving could change the calculation. A discounted Series 11 could also be worth considering alongside the SE 3 if a small premium gets you features you’ll use.
Be much more cautious with the Series 8, SE 2, and original Ultra: those models cannot run watchOS 27. The Series 9 is the oldest standard Apple Watch compatible with the latest software, while the Ultra 2 is the oldest supported Ultra and the SE 3 is the only supported SE. Missing the latest software doesn’t make an older watch unusable, but it makes it harder to recommend as a purchase today.
The Series 9, Series 10, and Ultra 2 can still be worth considering at sufficiently low prices. However, compatibility with today’s software doesn’t guarantee how many future upgrades they’ll receive. Weigh the savings against the watch’s age and features, rather than assuming every supported generation offers equally good value.






Apple Watch deals to avoid 

				
					

				
			
David Price / Foundry




Don’t let a bigger advertised discount tempt you into paying more for a cellular Apple Watch you won’t use. If your iPhone is usually nearby, a GPS model can already handle calls, messages, and notifications through your phone. It can also track runs, use Apple Pay, and play downloaded music without your iPhone. As our experience testing a cellular Apple Watch showed, the extra connectivity may add little to everyday use.
Cellular is worth considering if you regularly leave your iPhone behind and want to remain contactable without Wi-Fi, or you’re setting up a watch for a child without an iPhone. Otherwise, you could pay extra for the hardware and then add an ongoing mobile-plan charge for a feature you rarely need. You don’t have to activate a plan on a cellular model, so it can still be a good buy if its sale price matches or beats the GPS version. Our GPS versus cellular Apple Watch guide explains the trade-offs.
Check the rest of the configuration, too. A premium case material or expensive band can make a heavily discounted watch cost more than a simpler version that meets your needs. Judge offers against previous selling prices as well as the advertised reduction: a large saving from the original launch price doesn’t necessarily mean exceptional value. Check any spending requirements, contracts, trade-ins, or rebates attached to offers advertising a “free” Apple Watch.
Finally, check whether you’re buying a new, refurbished, or used watch, who is selling it, and what warranty and returns policy apply. For a used or refurbished model, check the stated battery condition and confirm that it has been removed from the previous owner’s account, with Activation Lock turned off. Make sure the watch is compatible with your iPhone before ordering.






How we choose Apple Watch deals
Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on Apple Watch reviews and everyday wear. We consider comfort, performance, battery life, charging, health and fitness features, and value – not just the specifications or advertised saving.
Our testing helps us explain which features are worth paying for. For example, our Series 12 review assessed battery life and charging performance alongside its newer health features. We also draw on everyday experience: our cellular Apple Watch testing examines whether staying connected without an iPhone justified the extra hardware and subscription costs.
We combine those findings with current prices and previous lows to judge whether an offer represents good value. We check the generation, case size, material, connectivity, and included band so that comparisons reflect what you’re actually buying. Older models can be worthwhile clearance purchases, but only when their prices make sense alongside discounted replacements.
Our Best Apple Watch guide explains why the most expensive model isn’t necessarily the right choice: your budget, wrist size, activities, and the features you need all matter.

This Black Friday, we’d watch the M4 iPad Air for a balance of performance and price, the A16 iPad for a worthwhile budget deal, and the M5 iPad Pro for buyers who need its premium capabilities. The new A20 Pro iPad mini, with its OLED display, also changes the calculation: we’d expect smaller initial discounts on the new arrival, while remaining A17 Pro stock could offer clearance bargains. Which iPad should you buy this Black Friday?


M4 iPad Air – Our best all-round choice

				
					

				
			
Apple Inc




The iPad Air offers a strong balance of performance, screen size, and price without the premium cost of the Pro. The 11-inch model suits buyers who prioritize portability, while the 13-inch version gives you more room for multitasking and creative work.
A good Black Friday discount could make either size an attractive purchase. Compare storage capacities carefully, though: a larger advertised saving on a high-capacity model isn’t necessarily better value if you don’t need the extra space. 
U.S. Black Friday price: At Amazon, you can already get a saving of $100 off some iPad Air models. iPad Pro – Best for demanding creative work

				
					

				
			
Apple Inc




The iPad Pro is the option for buyers who need Apple’s highest-end tablet performance and premium display. It comes in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes, but its capabilities – and price – will exceed what many people need for browsing, streaming, and everyday apps.
We’d look for a substantial saving rather than buy simply because it’s the most powerful iPad. Compare discounted M4 iPad Pro models, too: an older Pro could offer better value if its price is sufficiently below the equivalent M5 configuration. 
U.S. Black Friday price:  During October Prime Day, the 11-inch M5 Pro with 256GB was $1,099, saving $100. So far we’re seeing nearly $300 off a 1TB 11-inch iPad Pro.

iPad (A16) – Our budget choice, at the right price

				
					

				
			
Apple




The A16 iPad remains a capable option for browsing, streaming, schoolwork, and everyday use. However, Apple raised its starting price by $100/£100 in June, and it doesn’t support Apple Intelligence.
That makes the final purchase price particularly important. A modest discount from today’s higher asking price may still leave you paying more than this iPad previously cost. With a replacement expected early in 2027, we’d look for a substantial Black Friday saving and compare the price with discounted iPad Air models before buying.
U.S. Black Friday price: The 128GB A16 iPad was $399 during October Prime Day, saving $50 against its increased $449 price. Last Black Friday, it briefly reached $279. Should you buy an iPad now or wait for a better deal?

				
					

				
			
There’s an iPad for everyone.

Foundry




With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need an iPad immediately. But sales stretch across much of November, so an early offer can be worth taking if the price is competitive. Compare the exact generation, screen size, storage, and connectivity rather than waiting for Black Friday simply because a larger discount might appear.
If you’re buying an iPad Air and already plan to buy an Apple Pencil or keyboard later, Apple’s gift card may be worth waiting for. For the iPad Pro, check retailer prices first. The 11-inch M5 iPad Pro with 1TB has been listed at $299.01 off in the U.S. and £150 off in the U.K. at Amazon, both bigger savings than the Apple Gift Card.
Previous selling prices are particularly important this year because Apple raised iPad prices in June. During October Prime Day, the 128GB A16 iPad was $399, while the 11-inch M4 iPad Air with 128GB was $649. Both were discounted against Apple’s increased prices, but cost more than their regular prices before June. A saving from today’s asking price doesn’t necessarily mean you’re getting an exceptional bargain.
For the M4 iPad Air and M5 iPad Pro, we’d focus on finding a good price: We don’t expect replacements until 2027, as explained in our guide to the best time to buy an iPad. We’d be more cautious about the A16 iPad, which lacks Apple Intelligence and is expected to be replaced. Unless you find a substantial saving, waiting could get you a more capable entry-level model.
The new A20 Pro iPad mini presents a different decision. It has only just arrived, so we’d expect smaller initial discounts rather than immediate clearance-level savings. If you want its OLED display and newer processor, a modest reduction may still be worthwhile. If price matters more, compare remaining A17 Pro stock – but make sure the saving justifies choosing the older hardware.






Should you buy an older iPad? 

				
					

				
			
Foundry




An older iPad can be a good buy if its price reflects its age and the features you give up. Compare its actual selling price with the discounted price of its replacement, matching screen size, storage, and connectivity where possible. A large saving from an old launch price doesn’t necessarily make it better value.
The M3 iPad Air and M4 iPad Pro are worth considering at substantial clearance discounts. Both remain capable options, and you may get more benefit from a lower price or additional storage than from the latest processor. However, if the newer equivalent costs only slightly more, the saving may not justify choosing the older generation.
The A17 Pro iPad mini also deserves consideration now that the A20 Pro model has arrived. It supports Apple Intelligence and remains a capable compact tablet, but you miss the newer model’s OLED display, faster processor, and thinner, lighter design. We’d want a meaningful saving rather than a small reduction from its former asking price.
Be more cautious with much older models. Check whether they support the current version of iPadOS and the apps and features you need. Compatibility today doesn’t guarantee how many future software upgrades they’ll receive. Apple Intelligence support also varies: don’t assume every older Air, Pro, or mini includes it.
If you already own an Apple Pencil or keyboard, check compatibility before changing generations. Keeping compatible accessories could make an older iPad better value, while replacing them could erase part of your saving. Our iPad buying guide explains the differences between the ranges.






iPad deals to avoid
Check the exact configuration before comparing offers. Retailer listings can emphasize iPad, Air, or Pro without making the generation obvious. Confirm the chip, screen size, storage capacity, and whether you’re buying Wi-Fi or Wi-Fi + Cellular. A cheaper listing may be a different model rather than a better deal.
Don’t let a large advertised discount tempt you into paying for storage or connectivity you won’t use. A heavily reduced high-capacity or cellular iPad can still cost more than a simpler configuration that meets your needs. Compare the final purchase prices, rather than assuming the biggest saving represents the best value.
Check whether the price includes nano-texture glass, too. This optional finish (on the 1TB and 2TB M5 iPad Pro and the 256GB and 512GB A20 Pro iPad mini) reduces glare and makes fingerprints and oily smudges less noticeable, which can be useful if reflections make your iPad difficult to see in bright rooms or outdoors. It avoids much of the washed-out appearance associated with ordinary matte finishes, but contrast can drop at some viewing angles and the surface may be more scratch-sensitive. Availability depends on the model and storage configuration, so you could end up paying for both the finish and additional storage. If reflections rarely bother you, standard glass may be better value. Read our guide to nano-texture glass and whether you need it.
Our iPad buying guide considers cellular a luxury for most buyers. If you mainly use your iPad somewhere with Wi-Fi, you may get little benefit from the extra hardware. For occasional use elsewhere, sharing your iPhone’s connection through Personal Hotspot can be a more economical option.
Cellular makes more sense if you regularly need an independent connection while commuting or traveling; it also adds built-in GPS for accurate location tracking. Factor in any data-plan charges and compare the total cost of a contract with buying outright. A cellular model can still be worthwhile if its sale price matches or beats the equivalent Wi-Fi version—you don’t have to activate a data plan simply because the hardware is included.
Judge savings against previous selling prices as well as Apple’s current price. Following June’s price increases, a discounted iPad may still cost more than it did earlier in the year. Also distinguish a cash discount from a gift-card offer: a gift card doesn’t reduce the amount you pay for the iPad and is useful only if you’ll spend it.
Check what any bundle includes. A keyboard, case, or stylus doesn’t automatically make an offer better value, particularly if the accessories aren’t the versions you want. Read the conditions attached to “free” iPads, trade-in promotions, contracts, and rebates before comparing their total cost with buying outright.
Finally, check whether the iPad is new, refurbished, or used, who is selling it, and what warranty and returns policy apply. For used or refurbished models, look for information about battery condition and confirm that Activation Lock has been removed. Be cautious about devices that remain tied to a previous owner or an organization’s management system.






How we choose iPad deals
Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on iPad reviews and everyday use. We consider performance, display quality, portability, battery life, and accessory support alongside price to explain which iPads suit different buyers.
Our reviews help us assess whether paying more brings practical benefits. A faster processor or premium display may matter for demanding creative work, while a less expensive iPad can be perfectly capable of browsing, streaming, and schoolwork. We also consider the cost of keyboards, Apple Pencils, and other accessories when judging an iPad’s value.
We combine those findings with current prices and previous offers, matching the generation, screen size, storage, and connectivity so that comparisons reflect what you’re actually buying. Following Apple’s June price increases, we also consider earlier selling prices rather than relying solely on savings against today’s recommended price.
Older models can be worthwhile clearance purchases, but only when their prices make sense alongside newer alternatives. Our iPad buying guide explains the differences between the ranges, while our purchase-timing guide helps you decide whether to buy now or wait.
For more offers, visit our Black Friday coverage and our roundups of the best Mac deals, AirPods deals, and Apple Watch deals.

title: How to connect two or more external displays to an M1, M2, M3, M4, M5 or M6 MacBook or Neo
content:
Macworld






Black Friday deals are already appearing, and we’ve listed some of the best Display Link dock deals here, although keep reading the reviews and live price comparisons to find the best solution (and discount) for your needs.

While the higher-end MacBooks with M1/M2/M3/M4/M5 Pro and Max chips support multiple external displays, Apple’s lower-end range of MacBooks that use a standard M1 and M2 processor cannot natively connect more than one external monitor. The MacBook Neo is also limited to just one external monitor.
This is a massive limitation for these entry-level Macs: M1 MacBook, M2 MacBook and MacBook Neo. Apple’s M3 MacBook Air models do support two external monitors but only if the MacBook has its lid closed in what is known as Clamshell Mode. The M3 MacBook Pro supports a similar feature if at least the macOS Sonoma 14.6 update is installed. We explain how to run dual external displays on an M3 MacBook in a separate article.
Who will these Mac external monitor tips help?
• If your Mac has a plain (non-Pro or non-Max) M1 or M2 chip, or is the MacBook Neo, it is limited to using just one external monitor unless you follow our tips and workaround here.
• If your Mac has a plain (non-Pro or non-Max) M3 chip, it can only use two external monitors if its own lid is closed (so not showing its own screen) unless you follow our tips and workaround here.
• If your Mac has an M4, M5, M6, M4 Pro, M4 Max chip, it is limited to using two external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.
• If your Mac has an M5 Pro chip, it is limited to using three external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.
• If your Mac has an M5 Max chip, it is limited to using four external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.
The solutions below, however, allow for more than two external displays on plain M1, M2 Macs and MacBook Neo plus M3 Macs with their lids open if you want it. The base M4/M5 MacBook Air and M4/M5/M6 MacBook Pro models do natively support two displays with the lid open but if you want three or more displays for these MacBooks, then keep reading.
In each case, there’s a software download and a docking station, hub or adapter required. 
Later, we list our tested and recommended software and hardware solutions for adding more than one display to the plain M1, M2 and M3 Macs, plus MacBook Neo. You can jump straight to our list of the best DisplayLink docks if you know all about it. If not, read on a while.
The simplest solution is to get a USB graphics-enabled docking station or hub, sometimes called a DisplayLink Dock—and we’ve reviewed the best ones later in this article. USB graphics is a software-based technology (DisplayLink or InstantView) that compresses the video signals from the computer to the monitor, enabling you to connect multiple external displays to your M1/M2/M3 or Neo MacBook.
We cover the basics of how to connect your Mac to an external monitor.
Desktop Macs can be helped, too.
While the M1, M2 and Neo MacBooks natively support just one monitor, the desktop M1 Mac Mini and M2 Mac Mini do natively support up to two external monitors—one via the HDMI port and a second via USB-C. The M4 Mac mini supports up to three displays—two displays with up to 6K resolution at 60Hz over Thunderbolt and one display with up to 5K resolution at 60Hz over Thunderbolt or 4K resolution at 60Hz over HDMI.
Workaround: Install DisplayLink software drivers
You can use a combination of display technologies to get around the M1/M2/M3/Neo MacBooks’ single-monitor limitation. DisplayLink is the most common software solution that you pair with a compatible dock, and SiliconMotion’s InstantView is another. Note that the docks need to state DisplayLink or InstantView compatibility—you can’t just install DisplayLink drivers and hope they work with regular docks and hubs. Here, we’ll refer to them all as DisplayLink docks for brevity.
DisplayLink enable adapters or docks to output video over USB ports that would otherwise support only data connections, bypassing limitations on the number of screens a Mac can support natively (for example, the single-display limitation on base M1, M2, M3, and Neo Macs). Many multi-display docks use a combination of native USB-C Alternate Mode (native “Alt Mode” video output) and DisplayLink technology. This combination serves as a workaround to the M1/M2/M3/Neo platform supporting only a single external display via USB-C.
Note that DisplayLink requires a third-party driver to be installed on the Mac. In general, setup is straightforward. Some of the docks we review below offer the DisplayLink software when you first connect the dock to your Mac. The DisplayLink macOS app or DisplayLink Manager app are ways of enabling DisplayLink technology on macOS. The app is available as a standalone installer rather than through the mac App Store. There are download versions for macOS 26 Tahoe and earlier.
The initial InstantView setup is easier than DisplayLink with the hubs from Hyper and Satechi—but it suffers the same challenge that Apple’s software updates could disable it, which will entail installing a newer version and allowing the necessary security & privacy settings for screen recording, just as with DisplayLink. You can download the latest version of InstantView software here. The latest version supports macOS Golden Gate 27, Tahoe 26, Sequoia 15, Sonoma 14.
Neither software solution is complicated and both worked well in our tests as you can read below. There are some disadvantages to using DisplayLink and InstantView, which we explain in detail in the FAQ section below the dock chart, but none that should bother most users.

				
					

				
			This docking station supports three external displays via DisplayLink, while still allowing the MacBook to show its independent screen.
1. First, download the latest Mac DisplayLink driver. As stated above, some docks, do this for you but it’s always best to use the latest version.
DisplayLink Manager Graphics Connectivity App v. 17.1 is compatible with macOS Golden Gate 27, Tahoe 26, Sequoia 15, Sonoma 14. For macOS Ventura 13, you need version 14.2; and for Monterey 12, it’s version 1.11; for Big Sur 11, look for version 1.9, and v1.5 for Catalina 10.15. It can be managed via the DisplayLink icon in the Apple Menu bar.
Here’s the one fiddly part: you need to enable “Screen Recording” to allow the DisplayLink Manager app to capture pixels and send them to your USB peripheral. 
This can be found in System Preferences under Privacy in Security & Privacy; navigate to Screen Recording in the list on the left, then tick the Screen Recording permission for DisplayLink Manager after unlocking the padlock using your admin password. You may need to quit and restart DisplayLink Manager afterward. Don’t worry, DisplayLink isn’t recording your screen—this just lets it do its magic enabling multiple screens.
Installation is straightforward; take a look at the instructions here. Older versions did not support laptops’ closed-display/Clamshell Mode, but 1.8.1 and later do support Clamshell Mode if the MacBook is running macOS 11 or later.
There’s an option in DisplayLink manager to “launch at startup”, or you can drag the DisplayLink Manager to your Login Items in Users & Groups.
2. Then connect the MacBook to a DIsplayLink docking station—the dock must support DisplayLink, as all the reviewed products listed below do.
3. For the first screen you can connect via the dock’s DisplayPort, HDMI or USB-C/Thunderbolt port, and this will be handled natively by the M1/M2 MacBook. If you need to, you can use a USB-C to HDMI or DisplayPort adapter. If connecting to a MacBook Neo, use the rear 10Gbps USB 3 port.
The HDMI or DisplayPort output uses Alternate Mode (Alt Mode), and as it is basically a pipeline directly to the system’s native GPU, it will behave just like if you hooked up a USB-C to HDMI dongle to your laptop. This requires no user driver installation.
The second and third displays will rely on the DisplayLink software. DisplayLink uses an installed driver and the system CPU and GPU to convert graphics data on the system into data packets. That data is then sent over the cable as data packets and converted back to video information and output to the monitors via the DisplayLink chip in the docking station.
Which dock is best?
A docking station connects to your MacBook via Thunderbolt or USB-C. It then offers multiple ports that your laptop now has access to. These can include new display ports, such as HDMI, as well as Ethernet for wired Internet access, USB-C/Thunderbolt/USB-A ports at varying speeds, audio plugs, and card readers. A simpler hub or adapter has fewer ports but may have all the video or USB ports required. 
The main thing to remember here is that the dock, hub or adapter needs to support either DisplayLink or InstantView for the extra multi-screen magic to work. Non-DisplayLink docking stations are great if your MacBook can handle the number of screens you desire but you need more ports and functionality.
Docking station and hub manufacturers are now actively marketing their products as solutions to the M1/M2/M3/Neo external display limitation—docks have to support DisplayLink to work with the software. All the docks and hubs reviewed below require either the DisplayLink download or another similar software solution, such as InstantView, but no further hardware adapter except for the dock or hub itself. And of course, these hubs offer the usual multi-port benefits as well as the external monitor solution.
The best multiscreen hubs and adapters for Neo, M1, M2, M3, M4, M5 and M6 MacBooks
Below we have gathered the best dedicated hubs and docks for multiscreen M1/M2/M3/M4/M5/M6/Neo. Note that most of these listed (and tested) below use USB-C rather than Thunderbolt, so don’t benefit from the MacBook’s potential pro-level 40-80Gbps data bandwidth but are usually cheaper. If you require bandwidth higher than 10Gbps, go for a DisplayLink-supporting Thunderbolt dock. The MacBook Neo has USB-C rather than Thunderbolt so is limited to 10Gbps anyway but can use the Thunderbolt docks, too if you like as USB-C and Thunderbolt are compatible..
We have tested DisplayLink docks that can support up to five external displays and some that max out at two, which we expect will be plenty enough screen space for most people. You can use a five-screen DisplayLink dock even if you need only two monitors, and use the spare ports for other purposes.

Let’s begin with the DisplayLink dock that supports the most external displays: the Plugable UD-7400PD allows even M1 MacBook and Neo users to run up to five 4K displays at a 60Hz refresh rate. This is made possible by use of the latest Synaptics’ DisplayLink DL-7400 chipset. No other dock can match it. Although five displays is probably overkill for most users, financial and data analysts can’t have enough screens and will love it. You don’t have to add five displays, of course, but this dock is the one that will let you do so. It even offers something to the mighty M5 Max MacBook that can natively support four external displays; with the Plugable UD-7400PD it can move to five.
There are two HDMI ports (one HDMI 2.1 for 8K and one 2.0) plus three downstream USB-C ports to connect either those displays or other devices. There are two fast 10Gbps USB-A ports, speedy 2.5Gb Ethernet and an audio jack, but no SD card reader. At the front of the dock, one of the USB-C ports can output power to a connected device at 30W, which is perfect if you want to fast-charge an iPhone or even an iPad.
If you need faster bandwidth, the Satechi Thunderbolt 4 Docking Station with DisplayLink (reviewed below) boasts 40Gbps data transfer and supports four displays for the M3 MacBook Air (while shut in Clamshell Mode), but with it the M1 and M2 MacBooks are limited to three (one at 6K and two at 4K). 
IT managers will appreciate Plugable’s DockTag technology that works with the UD-7400PD, a web-based solution designed for hot-desking and real-time IT asset management in mixed-platform offices.

While plain M1/M2/Neo MacBooks are limited to three external displays using this dock when DisplayLink software is installed, M3/M4/M5/M6 and M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro/Max MacBooks can connect to four 4K at 60Hz. Other docks reviewed here also allow M1 and M2 Macs to connect to three displays, but what we really like about the Kensington SD5900T is its fast 40Gbps Thunderbolt 4 bandwidth rather than the usual 10Gbps USB-C docks. At present, there are no 80Gps Thunderbolt 5 DisplayLink docks. Note that the Neo uses 10Gbps USB-C rather than Thunderbolt, so is limited to that speed, although it will still work with Thunderbolt docks.
Two other docks—the Satechi Thunderbolt 4 Docking Station with DisplayLink and Plugable TBT-6950PD, both reviewed below—also offer Thunderbolt 4, but the Kensington SD5900T offers more flexibility on video ports, as well as boasting a few more than the other two. 
That Thunderbolt port connection also allows one of the three screens to be at 6K resolution (60Hz) while the other two via HDMI or DisplayLink will be 4K at 60Hz. Macs with a Pro or Max M-series chip can run two 4K/60Hz and two 6K/60Hz. Kensington sacrifices one of the potential Thunderbolt ports for an extra DisplayPort, while the Satechi and Plugable docks go with three downstream TB4 plus two HDMI. It does, however, offer an extra 10GBps/15W USB-C port at the front.
Its network port is 2.5Gb Ethernet compared to the 1Gb Ethernet on the Satechi and Plugable. It’s backwards compatible with Gigabit Ethernet so will work fine with standard wired networks.
If connecting to multiple monitors with the greatest flexibility is your principal goal, then the Kensington SD5900T is a great DisplayLink solution. If you want an extra 40Gbps Thunderbolt port, look to the Satechi and Plugable docks.

Foundry




However, there are ways around these plain M1/M2/M3 and Neo limitations, allowing you to run two or more external displays off your MacBook, which we will outline here. In each case, there’s a software download and a docking station, hub or adapter required. 
What you need to know about DisplayLink and InstantView
 FAQ 


1.
Does DisplayLink and InstantView block Netflix or other streaming content?
DisplayLink and InstantView are great at adding multiple monitors to M1, M2, M3 and Neo Macs, but there is a catch.
Some protected content in Netflix, AppleTV, Amazon Prime, Disney+ or YouTube TV and other streaming applications may not play. The video remains black while audio keeps playing.
This is all down to how the macOS interfaces the DisplayLink driver used to access graphics content. As soon as one DisplayLink-enabled screen is connected, protected content becomes unavailable on all screens.
This is down to the streaming platforms using High-bandwidth Digital Content Protection (HDCP), which is Intel-developed digital copy protection (Digital Rights Management or DRM) that prevents copying of digital audio and video content as it travels across connections.
Because macOS requires DisplayLink and InstantView to enable Screen Recording, HDCP moves in because it thinks you are actually trying to record the content rather than just display it on screen.





2.
How to enable streaming content when using DisplayLink or InstantView
To get round HDCP stopping your DisplayLink or InstantView setup showing Netflix, Amazon Prime and other streaming services, you may need to disconnect all the DisplayLink or InstantView screens, or switch to a browser other than Safari or Chrome (for example Opera or Firefox).
You can disable hardware acceleration in your browser to access the protected content.
On Google Chrome, go to Google Chrome settings, and click on “Advanced” and then select “System”. Here you can disable “Use hardware acceleration when available”.
Select “Relaunch” to activate the new setting.
If that doesn’t solve the black issue, disconnect the docking station, and try using the laptop’s build-in display or the direct video ports of the laptop.
Uninstalling the software is the ultimate solution.





3.
Does DisplayLink/InstantView impact display performance?
DisplayLink may introduce noticeable latency in some situations or on certain monitors, so high-end studios and professionals should look to a native solution that doesn’t require third-party software. 
Native video provides smoother, full-resolution lag-free video with higher refresh rates (4K at 240Hz), which makes it ideal for video editing and gaming. DisplayLink’s max is 60Hz—fine for most of us but nowhere near enough for video pros and gamers. 
As well as leaning on the CPU more, DisplayLink can introduce noticeable lag with rapidly changing content such as fast-moving video or gaming. It also suffers from restrictions to DRM (Digital Rights Management) protected content as used by streamers such as Netflix and Apple TV that DisplayLink can, as noted above.

title: UK Loses Secrecy Fight Over Apple 'Backdoor' Order
content:
Apple's challenge to a UK government demand for access to encrypted customer data can now be heard largely in public, after a tribunal rejected the Home Office's attempt to keep the order secret, according to the Financial Times.


The Investigatory Powers Tribunal today ruled that the British government had failed to demonstrate that confirming the demand would damage national security. The decision requires the Home Office to acknowledge that it served Apple with a technical capability notice (TCN), which is an order that can compel companies to make customer data accessible to UK security services, even when it is encrypted.

Financial Times, and discussions with U.S. officials had already departed significantly from that policy.

In its judgment, the tribunal said the combined effect was that anyone following the dispute already knew Apple had received a TCN. It described the suggestion that official acknowledgment would threaten national security or give a malicious actor fresh information as "fanciful."

title: Apple scrambles to address HomeView complaints
content:
Macworld





Since launching last week, Apple’s new HomeView hub has been beset by complaints. Multiple dissatisfied customers in multiple threads across multiple forums have reported issues covering areas as diverse as Music, Photos, device setup, Siri performance, and screen auto-brightness. But things are looking up, as Apple this week moves to address the problems.
As customers hoped, the first step includes a quick software update, which arrived Wednesday. In its release notes, Apple explains that HomeView Software Version 27.2.1 features “important bug fixes for your HomeView” specifically addressing these issues:
Setting up a Shared Album on the Photos face may prevent the device from downloading support for Siri, causing Siri to be unavailable
Pairing with an iPhone or iPad running the iOS or iPadOS 27.3 beta may cause Siri requests to fail
Connecting another home hub device (such as a HomePod or Apple TV) may unexpectedly remove HomeView from your home
HomeView should install software updates automatically, but you can force the process by updating your paired iPhone or iPad to the latest available version of iOS/iPadOS, opening the Home app, then going to More > Home Settings > Software Update > Update Now. Alternatively, open the Settings app on HomeView itself and go to System > Software Update > Update Software > Download and Install.
The three bugs above all sound frustrating, and they’re deceptively broad: the first and second, notably, are liable to essentially remove all voice control capacity if you’re unfortunate enough to trigger them. These fixes may therefore solve a wider range of complaints than the short list might suggest. It could be good news for customers reporting an inability to set timers via Siri, for example, or to make music start or stop playing.
Apple hasn’t made an official statement in response to the complaints, although the use of the phrase “important bug fixes” in these release notes is a fairly unambiguous acknowledgement that there have been problems. But the company has been prepared to offer advice in less public forums. One of the more positive stories shared earlier this week, for example, concluded happily with an Apple employee identifying the use of an iOS beta as the cause of the problem and a factory reset as the (successful) cure.
I visited Apple’s London headquarters this week to take a look at HomeView and some other smart-home products, and took the opportunity to speak to Apple representatives on this subject while I was there. They declined to offer a statement or to be quoted directly, but were quite forthcoming on possible causes and fixes.
Echoing the thoughts of my colleague Jason Cross (who delivered his first impressions of HomeView in the latest Macworld Podcast), they suggested that some of the problems might go away if customers updated the software (out of the box, you tend to find an early build on the first batch of a new product, which is likely to have been sitting in a warehouse for some time). They also discussed the use of iOS betas, and the potential for iCloud and Apple Music account mix-ups to cause some of the issues reported.
If you’ve got a HomeView that’s playing up, we recommend forcing the software update first of all to see if that helps. Then a trip to an Apple Store (or a call to Apple Support) is probably in order, because there are remedies you can try.
HomeView has had a bit of a cursed launch, but we should bear in mind that it is a new product in a new market for Apple. There were always going to be teething pains. The real test will be how well Apple responds to them.

content:
